blocks.text: If tools are how a model does things, resources are how it knows things. A resource is a piece of context a client can read, a file, a database record, a document, and hand to the model so it has real, current information to reason with, rather than relying only on what it already learned during training. This lesson goes deep on resources, building on the brief introduction from earlier in this module.
1. Resources Are for Reading, Never for Doing

blocks.alt: A resource is read-only compared against a tool, which takes action

blocks.text: The clearest way to tell a resource apart from a tool is to ask whether fetching it changes anything. Reading a file does not modify the file, checking a database record does not alter that record, this read-only nature is what makes resources fundamentally safer to expose than tools, there is no side effect to worry about, only the question of who should be allowed to see the content.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: Ask, if I fetch this twice, does anything change as a result, if not, it is almost certainly a resource, not a tool.

blocks.text: This safety property is exactly why resources typically require a lighter permission model than tools, reading rarely needs the same level of scrutiny as an action that can change something.

Some servers do apply access control even to reads, sensitive data still deserves protection, but the design space is simpler than it is for tools, since there is no action to authorize, only visibility.
2. Every Resource Has a URI

A resource is identified by a URI, exactly like the ones covered in the dedicated Resource URIs lesson in the MCP Resources module, file:///path/to/file.txt for a local file, or a custom scheme like db://orders/12345 for a database record. This URI is how a client refers to a specific resource when asking to read it.
This is exactly the same URI concept covered in depth in the Resource URIs lesson, a resource is never identified by a vague name alone, it always has this precise, structured identifier.
A URI never needs to be guessed, it always comes from the server itself, either through resources/list or through a resource template being filled in with a known value.
3. Listing Resources: resources/list

Just like tools, resources are discovered rather than hardcoded, a client calls resources/list to find out what a server currently offers, receiving back a list of URIs along with human-readable names and descriptions for each.

code.content:
# a client caching the resource list for the duration of a session
resource_list = client.list_resources()
cache["resources"] = resource_list

blocks.text: A large server might expose hundreds or thousands of resources, which is exactly why pagination, covered in its own dedicated lesson, matters for resources/list in practice.
4. Reading a Resource: resources/read

blocks.alt: A client sends resources/read to get content

blocks.text: Once a client knows a resource’s URI, it fetches the actual content with resources/read, the server returns the content, which might be plain text, structured data, or binary content depending on what the resource actually is.
The result of resources/read typically includes the resource’s URI, its MIME type, and its actual content, giving the client everything it needs to correctly interpret what was returned.
A client should always check the returned MIME type before assuming the content is plain, readable text, since a resource can just as easily be structured JSON or a binary blob.
5. Static vs Dynamic Resources

blocks.alt: A static resource is compared against a dynamic resource

blocks.text: A static resource has a fixed, predictable identity, a specific configuration file that always exists at the same URI. A dynamic resource is generated or discovered on the fly, like search results or a computed report, dynamic resources are covered in their own dedicated lesson in the MCP Resources module, but it is worth knowing upfront that not every resource is a simple, unchanging file.

code.content:
# static: always the same URI, fixed content source
"file:///config/settings.json"
# dynamic: generated per request
"search:///results?q=quarterly+report"

blocks.text: Neither kind is inherently better, a static resource is simpler and more predictable, a dynamic one is more flexible, the right choice depends entirely on what the underlying data actually looks like.
6. Resources vs Tools, Side by Side

blocks.alt: A resource is passive data while a tool is an active action

blocks.text: It helps to see the two concepts directly compared, since they are so often confused when someone first encounters MCP.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Tools","Resources"],"rows":[["Purpose","Take an action","Provide readable context"],["Side effects","Expected, often the whole point","None, purely read-only"],["Discovery method","tools/list","resources/list"],["Invocation method","tools/call","resources/read"]]}

blocks.text: Keeping this table in mind while designing a new server is a genuinely useful habit, whenever you are unsure which bucket a new piece of functionality belongs in, run it through each row.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question","Tools","Resources"],"rows":[["Does it change anything","Usually yes","Never"],["Needs strict permission review","Often yes","Sometimes, for sensitive content"]]}

blocks.text: When in doubt about a new feature, running through this comparison first saves time later, miscategorizing something as a tool when it should be a resource often leads to unnecessary permission friction down the line.
7. Resources vs Prompts

Resources are also easy to confuse with prompts at first, a resource is raw content to be read, a prompt, covered in the next lesson, is an instruction template meant to be filled in and sent as a message. A resource might well be pulled into a prompt as part of filling it in, but the two concepts serve different roles.
A simple test to keep them apart, a resource is content, a prompt is an instruction about what to do with content, they frequently work together but are not interchangeable.
Both resources and prompts ultimately end up as part of what the model sees, but they arrive there through different mechanisms and for different reasons.
8. How Resources Feed a Model’s Context

Once a resource is read, its content is typically inserted directly into the model’s context, alongside the conversation so far, giving the model fresh, specific information to reason about, this is exactly why resources matter so much for any task that depends on real, current data rather than the model’s general training knowledge.

code.content:
resource_content = client.read_resource("file:///notes.txt")
prompt = f"Here is some context: {resource_content['text']}\n\nAnswer the question using this context."

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["1","Discover resources via resources/list"],["2","Read the relevant one via resources/read"],["3","Insert its content into the model context"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Resource Descriptions Matter Just Like Tool Descriptions

A clear, specific description on a resource helps a client, or the model deciding what to fetch, understand what that resource actually contains before spending the effort to read it, a resource named report.txt with the description "quarterly sales report for Q2" is far more useful than one with no description at all.
This matters even more once a server exposes many resources at once, a client, or the model choosing what to read, benefits enormously from being able to tell resources apart at a glance.

code.content:
# vague vs specific resource descriptions
# vague: "a file"
# specific: "the project README describing setup instructions and architecture"

blocks.text: Treat writing a resource description the same way you would treat labeling a folder in a shared drive, the goal is for someone, or something, skimming the list to immediately understand what they will find inside.
10. Binary and Non-Text Resources

blocks.alt: A text resource is compared against a binary resource

blocks.text: Not every resource is plain text, a resource might be an image, a PDF, or another binary format, MCP supports this by allowing resource content to be returned as a base64-encoded blob alongside a MIME type, rather than assuming everything is readable text.
A client needs to check the MIME type before deciding how to handle a resource’s content, text/plain can be shown directly, application/pdf needs different handling entirely.

blocks.title: A practical note
blocks.content: Base64 encoding adds roughly a third to the raw size of binary content, worth remembering when budgeting context space for a resource that includes an image or document.

blocks.text: 11. Resources Can Be Large, Budget Accordingly

A resource might contain far more content than the model’s context window can comfortably hold, this is exactly why the Context Windows and Context Compression lessons in the Context Management module matter so much in practice, a client often needs to summarize or truncate a large resource before handing it to the model.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Before reading a resource that might be very large, check whether a summary or a smaller, more targeted resource exists instead, rather than pulling in the entire thing by default.

blocks.text: This is one more reason resources and context management, covered in the dedicated module later in this curriculum, are so closely linked, a resource that is technically available is not always wise to read in full.
A useful habit is asking, before reading a resource, roughly how large is this likely to be, a quick size check can prevent an unpleasant surprise once the content actually arrives.
12. Resources Can Change Over Time

The content behind a given URI is not necessarily fixed forever, a file can be edited, a database record can be updated, MCP supports a subscription mechanism so a client can be notified when a resource it cares about changes, covered fully in the Resource Versioning lesson in the MCP Resources module.

blocks.title: Where subscriptions come in
blocks.content: A client that subscribes to a resource is notified automatically when its content changes, rather than needing to repeatedly re-read it just to check.

blocks.text: 13. Resource Templates for Families of Resources

blocks.alt: A resource template produces resource instance 1 and resource instance 2

blocks.text: Rather than listing every single resource individually, a server can expose a resource template, a parameterized URI pattern like file:///{path} that describes a whole family of resources at once, this is covered fully in the Resource Templates lesson in the MCP Resources module, but it is worth knowing resources do not always need to be enumerated one by one.

blocks.title: A quick preview
blocks.content: A single template like notes:///{date} can represent every note a user has ever written, without the server needing to list each one individually.

blocks.text: 14. Security Considerations for Resources

Because a resource can expose sensitive content, private files, confidential records, a server needs to think carefully about which resources a given caller is actually allowed to read, this is covered in full in the Resource Security lesson in the MCP Resources module and the broader Authentication & Security module.
A server exposing a resource for every file on a machine, without any access control, risks leaking far more than intended, careful scoping here matters as much as it does for tools.
15. A Worked Example
Trace a simple flow, discovering a project’s resources, reading one specific file, and handing its content to a model to answer a question about it.

code.content:
resources = client.list_resources()
readme = next(r for r in resources if r["uri"].endswith("README.md"))
content = client.read_resource(readme["uri"])
answer = model.ask(f"Based on this file: {content['text']}, what does this project do?")

blocks.text: Notice this is the exact same discover-then-fetch pattern used throughout MCP, whether for tools, resources, or, as the next lesson covers, prompts.
This exact pattern generalizes to almost any task that begins with needing real, specific information before a model can answer well, discover, read, then reason.
16. Common Mistakes When Working With Resources

items: Confusing a resource with a tool, and trying to "call" a resource instead of reading it, or vice versa.
Writing a resource description so vague that a client cannot tell whether it is worth reading before fetching it.
Reading an enormous resource without considering the model’s context window, and blowing the budget on a single piece of context.
Assuming resource content never changes, and never checking for updates on a resource that is actually being edited elsewhere.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is treating every resource as if it were static and never checking whether its content might have changed since it was last read.
17. Practice: Design Resources for a Notes App
Sketch what resources a simple notes-taking MCP server might expose, one URI scheme for individual notes, and one for a list of all notes, then write out what the description for each would say.

code.content:
resources = [
    {"uri": "notes:///2026-07-07", "description": "Note from July 7, 2026"},
    {"uri": "notes:///all", "description": "A list of every saved note"},
]

blocks.text: Once you have sketched these two resource types, consider whether the notes:///all resource should be static or dynamic, and why that choice matters for how a client should treat its content.

blocks.title: One more thing to try
blocks.content: Sketch how a resource template might replace listing every individual note URI by hand, using a single pattern like notes:///{date} instead.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A resource is readable context, identified by a URI, discovered through resources/list and fetched through resources/read, kept deliberately separate from tools since it has no side effects, and feeding directly into a model’s context so it can reason with real, current information.

This lesson builds on the brief introduction to resources earlier in this module, and connects forward to Prompts next, the third and final piece of what a server can expose, reusable instruction templates rather than raw content or actions.

The resource template concept from the newly added section becomes especially valuable once a server needs to expose a large, growing family of similar resources, rather than declaring each one individually.

Keep the security considerations from the newly added section in mind as you move forward, a resource that seems harmless in isolation can still leak sensitive information if access is not scoped thoughtfully.
